Abstract: Stiff person syndrome (SPS) has been associated
with autoimmune diseases, such as Type 1 diabetes mellitus
and autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis),
among others. The association of SPS with hyperthyroidism is
extremely rare. We describe a patient with uncontrolled
Graves’ disease and undiagnosed SPS, who presented initially
with acute ataxia simulating a cerebrovascular accident. Ini-
tiation of immunosuppressive therapy dramatically improved
the patient’s Graves’ disease within 2 weeks but the neurolog-
ical symptoms were not alleviated after a follow-up period of
3 years. © 2007 Movement Disorder Society

CASE DESCRIPTION
A middle age Chinese woman presented initially with
signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism and was subse-
quently diagnosed to have Graves’ disease. She was treated
with carbimazole with little improvement of her thyroid
condition. A few months later, she presented with the sud-
den onset of slurred speech and rapidly progressing un-
steady gait and was admitted for a probable cerebrovascular
accident. She also complained of neck stiffness and back-
ache about 2 weeks prior to her hospitalization . Examina-
tion revealed sinus tachycardia (heart rate 100/min), tem-
perature of 37°C, and a small diffusely enlarged nontender
goiter. She was alert and oriented, was noted to be dysar-
thric, with bilateral rotatory and jerk nystagmus, dysmetria,
dysdiadochokinesia and marked truncal ataxia. She had an
increased extensor tone in her neck and trunk. No stimulus-
induced or spontaneous bodily spasms were present .
Strength in her proximal muscles was slightly reduced, and
the sensory examination was normal. Her reﬂexes were not
increased with bilateral ﬂexor plantar response. There was
no ophthalmopathy or dermopathy. Despite carbimazole
treatment, her thyroid function tests revealed severe thyro-
toxicosis (FT4 73.2 (9.6 –19.1 pmol/L), TSH /H110210.006
(0.36 –3.24 mU/L). Her thyroid antibody proﬁle was con-
sistent with Graves’ disease [Thyrototropin-binding inhibi-
tory immunoglobulin (TBII) 28 (0 –1.5 U/L), thyroid per-
oxidase antibody (TPOAb) /H110223,000 (0 – 60 U/mL),
thyroglobulin antibody (TgAb) /H110222,000 (0 – 60 U/mL),

thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) /H110223,077 (50 –
179%)] (Table 1).
Her father had Type 2 diabetes mellitus but there was
no family history of thyroid disease or multiple sclerosis.
Blood count, prothrombin and partial-thromboplastin
times, liver and renal function tests, serum electrolytes,
creatine kinase, and aldolase were normal. Brain and
cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging studies were
unremarkable. Magnetic resonance spectroscopic studies
revealed a reduced myo-inositol and total choline in the
frontal gray matter and parieto-occipital white matter.
CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, and mammo-
gram revealed no abnormality. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF)
examination was normal except for the presence of an
oligoclonal band. Electromyography of the axial muscles
revealed continuous electrical discharges even in a re-
laxed state. Nerve conduction tests were normal.
Her glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody (GAD Ab)
levels were grossly elevated [ /H11022187 (0 –9.5 U/L)]. An-
tiamphiphysin antibody was not carried out . She was
given a trial of plasmapheresis over 3 days, and subse-
quently a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin
therapy (IVIG) at 0.4 g/kg/day with no improvement of

her motor function. However, the immunosuppression
produced a signiﬁcant effect on her hyperthyroidism,
with a rapid decrease in her thyroid hormone levels
within 2 weeks (Table 1).
She subsequently declined steroid and other therapies.
We followed her up for 3 years, and while she was still
severely disabled, her motor function had remained sta-
ble. Since the initial immunosuppression, her Graves’
disease had been well controlled with a low dose of
carbimazole. Her TBII had decreased further but was still
positive [3.5 U/L (0 –1.5)].

The patient did not have ataxia
and was not treated with antithyroid medication.
7 Multiple
treatments with immunoglobulins, steroids, and azathioprine
improved both the thyroid and neurological symptoms.
While it is well recognized that SPS can be associated
with auto-immune thyroid disorders, it is unknown why
Graves’ disease is so rarely associated with the condition.
This could be due to the differential accessibility of GAD to
the immune system, or the humoral and cellular responses
to GAD65 may differ between the two diseases. However,
since in Graves’ disease, there is a Th-2 response with the
TSH receptor as the primary antigen, the production of TSI
may provide a plausible immunological reason for it to
coexist with SPS, which is also a Th-2 mediated disease.
1 It
is possible that in select at-risk patients, certain unknown
triggers could have led to a loss of T cell tolerance to GAD
and the TSH receptor, leading to activation of Th-2 activity.
However, onset of muscle stiffness in SPS may be insidious
as synaptic GABA-ergic transmission may take a while to
get progressively impaired, while in Graves’ disease, the
stimulation of the TSH receptor by TSI can produce imme-
diate clinically recognizable symptoms. The mechanism
underlying our patient’s presentation with acute cerebellar
symptoms, and the differential involvement of cerebral me-
tabolites (sparing the cerebellum) on magnetic resonance
spectroscopic studies is unclear . As the patient has been
monitored for more than 3 years, the possibility of an
associated paraneoplastic disease is unlikely. Hence we did
not test for antiamphiphysin antibody, which is associated
with breast cancer.
8 However, we have demonstrated the
presence of anti-GAD antibody and oligoclonal immuno-
globulin G (IgG) (in CSF), both of these antibodies are
commonly seen in the majority of patients with SPS.
8
In conclusion, our case highlights that an acute cere-
bellar syndrome in Graves’ disease can be associated
with SPS, and immunotherapy can effectively alleviate
symptoms of Graves’ disease with little impact on the
neurological function.
